claim: Aversive stimuli, including foot-shocks, excite LHb neurons in mice.
source: We observe that aversive stimuli, including foot-shocks, excite LHb neurons and promote escape behaviors in mice.
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing foot-shock-driven excitation of LHb neurons (Figure 1B-D) and calcium imaging showing fluorescence transients in response to foot-shocks (Figure 1A).

claim: Aversive stimuli promote escape behaviors in mice.
source: We observe that aversive stimuli, including foot-shocks, excite LHb neurons and promote escape behaviors in mice.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing mice rapidly escaped to the opposite compartment following foot-shocks (Figure 1A).

claim: Foot-shock-driven excitation within the LHb requires glutamatergic signaling from the LH.
source: The foot-shock-driven excitation within the LHb requires glutamatergic signaling from the LH, but not from the midbrain.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments showing that local CNO infusion in mice expressing DREADDi in LH→LHb significantly reduced foot-shock-mediated excitation (Figure 2D).

claim: Foot-shock-driven excitation within the LHb does not require glutamatergic signaling from the midbrain.
source: The foot-shock-driven excitation within the LHb requires glutamatergic signaling from the LH, but not from the midbrain.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic silencing experiments showing that local CNO infusion in mice expressing DREADDi in VTA→LHb did not reduce foot-shock-mediated excitation (Figure 2C).

claim: The hypothalamic excitatory projection predominates over LHb neurons monosynaptically innervating aversion-encoding midbrain GABA cells.
source: This hypothalamic excitatory projection predominates over LHb neurons monosynaptically innervating aversion-encoding midbrain GABA cells.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons presented lower I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios and larger maximal I-AMPA compared to other LHb cell targets (Figure 3B).

claim: Selective chemogenetic silencing of the LH-to-LHb pathway impairs aversion-driven escape behaviors.
source: Finally, the selective chemogenetic silencing of the LH-to-LHb pathway impairs aversion-driven escape behaviors.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing mice expressing DREADDi in LH→LHb escaped with higher latencies and increased shuttling failure rate (Figure 4B) and had larger escape latencies in the looming test (Figure 4C).

claim: Mice rapidly escape to the compartment opposite to the one of shock delivery across trials.
source: Across trials, mice rapidly escaped to the compartment opposite to the one of shock delivery (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing escape latencies and failures across 30 trials (Figure 1A).

claim: Foot-shocks (0.3 mA) evoke escape behavior along with time-locked fluorescent transients within the LHb.
source: Foot-shocks (0.3 mA), and aversive air-puffs (painless stimulus), evoked escape behavior (i.e. phasic increase in locomotion) along with time-locked fluorescent transients within the LHb (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing calcium transients in LHb neurons time-locked to foot-shocks (Figure 1A).

claim: Aversive air-puffs evoke escape behavior along with time-locked fluorescent transients within the LHb.
source: Foot-shocks (0.3 mA), and aversive air-puffs (painless stimulus), evoked escape behavior (i.e. phasic increase in locomotion) along with time-locked fluorescent transients within the LHb (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing calcium transients in LHb neurons time-locked to air-puffs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).

claim: A progressive increase in locomotion in absence of foot-shock does not modify the fluorescence signal measured from the LHb.
source: Notably, a progressive increase in locomotion in absence of foot-shock, artificially promoted using the rotarod, did not modify the fluorescence signal measured from the LHb (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data comparing calcium transients during foot-shock versus rotarod-induced locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: There is a relationship between LHb activity and escape behavior.
source: Therefore, simultaneous monitoring of fluorescence and behavior suggests a relationship between LHb activity and escape (Lawson et al., 2014; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007).
evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing time-locked calcium transients during escape behavior and cited literature (Lawson et al., 2014; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007).

claim: Foot-shocks lead to fast (~60 ms) and phasic increase (~100 ms) in action potentials in ~50% of neurons recorded across the LHb.
source: Foot-shocks (hindpaw delivery) led to fast (~60 ms) and phasic increase (~100 ms) in action potentials in ~50% of neurons recorded across the LHb (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo single-unit electrophysiology data showing foot-shock responses in LHb neurons (Figure 1B-D).

claim: Local infusion of glutamate receptors antagonists (APV and NBQX) diminishes foot-shock-driven excitation of LHb neurons.
source: Local infusion of glutamate receptors antagonists (APV and NBQX) diminished foot-shock-driven excitation of LHb neurons, without altering baseline firing, indicating the glutamatergic nature of the response (Figure 1E, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by in vivo pharmacology data showing reduced foot-shock responses after NBQX/AP5 application (Figure 1E-F).

claim: Local infusion of glutamate receptors antagonists (APV and NBQX) does not alter baseline firing of LHb neurons.
source: Local infusion of glutamate receptors antagonists (APV and NBQX) diminished foot-shock-driven excitation of LHb neurons, without altering baseline firing, indicating the glutamatergic nature of the response (Figure 1E, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by in vivo pharmacology data showing no change in baseline firing after NBQX/AP5 application (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).

claim: Foot-shock-driven excitation of LHb neurons is glutamatergic in nature.
source: Local infusion of glutamate receptors antagonists (APV and NBQX) diminished foot-shock-driven excitation of LHb neurons, without altering baseline firing, indicating the glutamatergic nature of the response (Figure 1E, Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutamate receptor antagonists diminish the foot-shock response.

claim: Glutamatergic projections from the medial ventral tegmentum (mVTA) in the midbrain innervate almost-entirely the LHb.
source: Glutamatergic projections from the medial ventral tegmentum (mVTA) in the midbrain and the lateral hypothalamus (LH) innervate almost-entirely the LHb (Stamatakis et al., 2013; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Barker et al., 2016; Kunwar et al., 2015; Root et al., 2014a; 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016), indicating their potential implication in conveying aversive information onto habenular neurons.
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Stamatakis et al., 2013; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Barker et al., 2016; Kunwar et al., 2015; Root et al., 2014a; 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016).

claim: Glutamatergic projections from the lateral hypothalamus (LH) innervate almost-entirely the LHb.
source: Glutamatergic projections from the medial ventral tegmentum (mVTA) in the midbrain and the lateral hypothalamus (LH) innervate almost-entirely the LHb (Stamatakis et al., 2013; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Barker et al., 2016; Kunwar et al., 2015; Root et al., 2014a; 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016), indicating their potential implication in conveying aversive information onto habenular neurons.
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Stamatakis et al., 2013; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Barker et al., 2016; Kunwar et al., 2015; Root et al., 2014a; 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016).

claim: mVTA and LH projections to the LHb are potentially implicated in conveying aversive information onto habenular neurons.
source: Glutamatergic projections from the medial ventral tegmentum (mVTA) in the midbrain and the lateral hypothalamus (LH) innervate almost-entirely the LHb (Stamatakis et al., 2013; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Barker et al., 2016; Kunwar et al., 2015; Root et al., 2014a; 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016), indicating their potential implication in conveying aversive information onto habenular neurons.
evidence: Inferred from anatomical connectivity and the role of LHb in aversion processing.

claim: Optical stimulation of CoChR-expressing mVTA terminals in acute slices evokes inward glutamatergic currents onto recorded neurons across the LHb.
source: Optical stimulation (1 ms; 470 nm) of CoChR-expressing mVTA or LH terminals (VTA→LHb and LH→LHb respectively), in acute slices, evoked inward glutamatergic currents onto recorded neurons (−50 mV) across the LHb (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing light-evoked currents from VTA→LHb terminals (Figure 2A).

claim: Optical stimulation of CoChR-expressing LH terminals in acute slices evokes inward glutamatergic currents onto recorded neurons across the LHb.
source: Optical stimulation (1 ms; 470 nm) of CoChR-expressing mVTA or LH terminals (VTA→LHb and LH→LHb respectively), in acute slices, evoked inward glutamatergic currents onto recorded neurons (−50 mV) across the LHb (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing light-evoked currents from LH→LHb terminals (Figure 2B).

claim: Optogenetic activation of VTA→LHb is sufficient to produce place aversion in behaving mice.
source: Moreover, in behaving mice, optogenetic activation of either VTA→LHb or LH→LHb was sufficient to produce place aversion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) (Root et al., 2014a; Stamatakis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by real-time place aversion behavioral data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and cited literature (Root et al., 2014a; Stamatakis et al., 2016).

claim: Optogenetic activation of LH→LHb is sufficient to produce place aversion in behaving mice.
source: Moreover, in behaving mice, optogenetic activation of either VTA→LHb or LH→LHb was sufficient to produce place aversion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) (Root et al., 2014a; Stamatakis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by real-time place aversion behavioral data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and cited literature (Root et al., 2014a; Stamatakis et al., 2016).

claim: VTA→LHb and/or LH→LHb can underlie aversive processing in the LHb and escape behaviors.
source: This supports the notion that VTA→LHb and/or LH→LHb can underlie aversive processing in the LHb and escape behaviors.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic sufficiency data showing place aversion.

claim: Application of CNO promptly reduces LH→LHb light-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents in acute slices.
source: Indeed, in acute slices, application of the DREADDi agonist clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) promptly reduced LH→LHb light-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents and increased the paired-pulse ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing CNO-mediated reduction of opto-evoked EPSCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C).

claim: Application of CNO increases the paired-pulse ratios of LH→LHb light-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents in acute slices.
source: Indeed, in acute slices, application of the DREADDi agonist clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) promptly reduced LH→LHb light-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents and increased the paired-pulse ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing CNO-mediated increase in paired-pulse ratios (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Local CNO infusion in mice expressing DREADDi in VTA→LHb does not alter foot-shock-mediated excitation of LHb neurons.
source: When recording LHb neuronal activity in vivo in anesthetized animals, local CNO infusion in mice expressing DREADDi in the LH→LHb, but not in the VTA→LHb, significantly reduced foot-shock-mediated excitation without altering baseline activity (Figure 2C and Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing no change in foot-shock responses after CNO application in VTA→LHb DREADDi mice (Figure 2C).

claim: Local CNO infusion in mice expressing DREADDi in LH→LHb significantly reduces foot-shock-mediated excitation of LHb neurons without altering baseline activity.
source: When recording LHb neuronal activity in vivo in anesthetized animals, local CNO infusion in mice expressing DREADDi in the LH→LHb, but not in the VTA→LHb, significantly reduced foot-shock-mediated excitation without altering baseline activity (Figure 2C and Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing reduced foot-shock responses after CNO application in LH→LHb DREADDi mice (Figure 2D).

claim: Retrogradely-labeled and optically-tagged LHb-projecting LH neurons are foot-shock responsive.
source: Consistently, retrogradely-labeled and optically-tagged LHb-projecting LH neurons were foot-shock responsive (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo electrophysiology data showing foot-shock responses in opto-tagged LH neurons projecting to LHb (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D-E).

claim: LHb-to-GABA cells are mostly located in the lateral portion of the LHb.
source: LHb-to-GABA cells were mostly located in the lateral portion of the LHb, in contrast to those projecting to DA- and 5HT neurons that were medially-located (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A [Meye et al., 2016]).
evidence: Supported by anatomical mapping data from rabies tracing experiments (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and cited literature (Meye et al., 2016).

claim: LHb cells projecting to DA neurons are medially-located.
source: LHb-to-GABA cells were mostly located in the lateral portion of the LHb, in contrast to those projecting to DA- and 5HT neurons that were medially-located (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A [Meye et al., 2016]).
evidence: Supported by anatomical mapping data from rabies tracing experiments (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and cited literature (Meye et al., 2016).

claim: LHb cells projecting to 5HT neurons are medially-located.
source: LHb-to-GABA cells were mostly located in the lateral portion of the LHb, in contrast to those projecting to DA- and 5HT neurons that were medially-located (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A [Meye et al., 2016]).
evidence: Supported by anatomical mapping data from rabies tracing experiments (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and cited literature (Meye et al., 2016).

claim: LH→LHb opto-stimulation leads to inward (−60 mV, I-AMPA) and outward current responses (+10 mV, I-GABA) in output-identified LHb neurons.
source: When recording from these output-identified LHb neurons in acute slices, we found that LH→LHb opto-stimulation led to inward (−60 mV, I-AMPA) and outward current responses (+10 mV, I-GABA) (Herrera et al., 2016; Stamatakis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing both excitatory and inhibitory currents (Figure 3B) and cited literature (Herrera et al., 2016; Stamatakis et al., 2016).

claim: LH synapses onto LHb-to-GABA neurons have high degree of connectivity (~90%).
source: LH synapses onto LHb-to-GABA and LHb-to-DA had high degree of connectivity (~90% and ~80% respectively) in contrast to those projecting to LHb-to-5HT neurons (~50%) (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing connectivity rates (Figure 3B).

claim: LH synapses onto LHb-to-DA neurons have high degree of connectivity (~80%).
source: LH synapses onto LHb-to-GABA and LHb-to-DA had high degree of connectivity (~90% and ~80% respectively) in contrast to those projecting to LHb-to-5HT neurons (~50%) (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing connectivity rates (Figure 3B).

claim: LH synapses onto LHb-to-5HT neurons have lower degree of connectivity (~50%).
source: LH synapses onto LHb-to-GABA and LHb-to-DA had high degree of connectivity (~90% and ~80% respectively) in contrast to those projecting to LHb-to-5HT neurons (~50%) (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing connectivity rates (Figure 3B).

claim: LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons present lower I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios compared to other LHb cell targets.
source: The LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons presented lower I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios, and larger maximal I-AMPA compared to other LHb cell targets (Figure 3B), suggesting that LH excitation predominates over LHb neurons synapsing onto downstream midbrain GABA cells.
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios (Figure 3B).

claim: LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons present larger maximal I-AMPA compared to other LHb cell targets.
source: The LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons presented lower I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios, and larger maximal I-AMPA compared to other LHb cell targets (Figure 3B), suggesting that LH excitation predominates over LHb neurons synapsing onto downstream midbrain GABA cells.
evidence: Supported by in vitro electrophysiology data showing maximal I-AMPA values (Figure 3B).

claim: LH excitation predominates over LHb neurons synapsing onto downstream midbrain GABA cells.
source: The LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons presented lower I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios, and larger maximal I-AMPA compared to other LHb cell targets (Figure 3B), suggesting that LH excitation predominates over LHb neurons synapsing onto downstream midbrain GABA cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LH→LHb-to-GABA neurons have lower I-GABA/I-AMPA ratios and larger maximal I-AMPA.

claim: Control animals successfully shuttle to the compartment opposite to the one of shock delivery with short latencies across trials after CNO injection.
source: Control (CTRL; rAAV-EF1α-td-Tomato) animals, after CNO injection, successfully shuttled to the compartment opposite to the one of shock delivery with short latencies across trials.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing escape latencies in control mice (Figure 4B).

claim: Mice expressing DREADDi in LH→LHb escape with higher latencies and increased shuttling failure rate.
source: Instead, mice expressing DREADDi in LH→LHb escaped with higher latencies, along with increased shuttling failure rate (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing increased escape latencies and failures in DREADDi mice (Figure 4B).

claim: Silencing VTA→LHb projections does not alter escape latencies or failures.
source: In contrast, no difference in latencies or failures was detected when silencing VTA→LHb projections consistent with the lack of contribution to foot-shock mediated LHb excitation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing no difference in escape behavior when silencing VTA→LHb (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Silencing the LH→LHb synapses does not alter locomotion in an open field.
source: Importantly, silencing the LH→LHb synapses did not alter locomotion in an open field, nor pain perception, measured with the hot-plate test (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing no difference in open field locomotion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Silencing the LH→LHb synapses does not alter pain perception measured with the hot-plate test.
source: Importantly, silencing the LH→LHb synapses did not alter locomotion in an open field, nor pain perception, measured with the hot-plate test (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing no difference in hot-plate latency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: CTRL mice rapidly escape from the arena center to a 'safe' area (nest) when exposed to a projected shadow mimicking predator attack.
source: When exposing CTRL mice, after CNO injection, to such paradigm, they rapidly escaped from the arena center to a 'safe' area (nest) (Figure 4C and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from the looming test showing rapid escape in control mice (Figure 4C).

claim: LH→LHb DREADDi mice have significantly larger escape latencies in the looming test.
source: In contrast LH→LHb DREADDi mice had significant larger escape latencies (Figure 4C and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from the looming test showing increased escape latencies in DREADDi mice (Figure 4C).

claim: The LH→LHb projection plays a crucial role in guiding escape, an evolutionary conserved innate response to a threat.
source: Altogether, these data attribute to the LH→LHb projection the crucial role in guiding escape, an evolutionary conserved innate response to a threat.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data showing impaired escape when LH→LHb is silenced.

claim: The lateral habenula (LHb) encodes disappointment and the negative value of a stimulus.
source: The lateral habenula (LHb), through the computing of its incoming inputs (i.e. basal ganglia, hypothalamus, midbrain), encodes disappointment and the negative value of a stimulus (Hong and Hikosaka, 2008; Knowland et al., 2017; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; Root et al., 2014b; Shabel et al., 2012; Stamatakis et al., 2016; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Hong and Hikosaka, 2008; Knowland et al., 2017; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; Root et al., 2014b; Shabel et al., 2012; Stamatakis et al., 2016; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017).

claim: Glutamatergic LHb neurons directly innervate midbrain GABA cells.
source: Glutamatergic LHb neurons directly innervate midbrain GABA cells, and indirectly inhibit dopamine cells, two neuronal populations known to respond to aversive stimuli (Brischoux et al., 2009; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Brischoux et al., 2009; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012).

claim: Glutamatergic LHb neurons indirectly inhibit dopamine cells.
source: Glutamatergic LHb neurons directly innervate midbrain GABA cells, and indirectly inhibit dopamine cells, two neuronal populations known to respond to aversive stimuli (Brischoux et al., 2009; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Brischoux et al., 2009; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012).

claim: Midbrain GABA cells and dopamine cells respond to aversive stimuli.
source: Glutamatergic LHb neurons directly innervate midbrain GABA cells, and indirectly inhibit dopamine cells, two neuronal populations known to respond to aversive stimuli (Brischoux et al., 2009; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Brischoux et al., 2009; Stamatakis and Stuber, 2012; Tan et al., 2012).

claim: A subset of habenular axons innervates aversion-encoding cortex-projecting dopamine neurons.
source: Notably, a subset of habenular axons also innervates aversion-encoding cortex-projecting dopamine neurons (Balcita-Pedicino et al., 2011; Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Balcita-Pedicino et al., 2011; Lammel et al., 2012).

claim: The LHb is a brain center encoding aversion mostly through the inhibition of the reward system.
source: These findings support a scenario in which the LHb is a brain center encoding aversion mostly through the inhibition of the reward system (Ji and Shepard, 2007).
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity and function of LHb with reward-related circuits, supported by cited literature (Ji and Shepard, 2007).

claim: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the medial portion of the ventral tegmental area (mVTA) innervate the LHb.
source: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the medial portion of the ventral tegmental area (mVTA), innervate the LHb (Herkenham and Nauta, 1977).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Herkenham and Nauta, 1977).

claim: Afferents from the LH and mVTA to the LHb are mostly excitatory.
source: Both the LH and the mVTA contain heterogeneous neuronal populations, but afferents to the LHb are mostly excitatory (Root et al., 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Root et al., 2014b; Stamatakis et al., 2016).

claim: LH and mVTA populations respond to negative events and contribute to shape aversive behaviors including escape.
source: Notably, such LH and mVTA populations respond to negative events and contribute to shape aversive behaviors including escape (Morales and Margolis, 2017; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; González et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Morales and Margolis, 2017; Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; González et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015).

claim: Escape behavior is an innate (non-conditioned) response crucial for survival.
source: Unexpected threats drive escape behavior, an innate (non-conditioned) response crucial for survival (Fadok et al., 2017; Mongeau et al., 2003); yet the required neurocircuitry guiding such behavioral response is unclear.
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Fadok et al., 2017; Mongeau et al., 2003) and established knowledge.

claim: The neurocircuitry guiding escape behavior in response to unexpected threats is unclear.
source: Unexpected threats drive escape behavior, an innate (non-conditioned) response crucial for survival (Fadok et al., 2017; Mongeau et al., 2003); yet the required neurocircuitry guiding such behavioral response is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to the current study.

claim: Habenula lesions reduce reward omission-driven inhibition of DA neurons.
source: Notably, while habenula lesions reduced reward omission-driven inhibition of DA neurons, it left instead intact the inhibitory response to aversive stimuli (Tian and Uchida, 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Tian and Uchida, 2015).

claim: Habenula lesions leave intact the inhibitory response of DA neurons to aversive stimuli.
source: Notably, while habenula lesions reduced reward omission-driven inhibition of DA neurons, it left instead intact the inhibitory response to aversive stimuli (Tian and Uchida, 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Tian and Uchida, 2015).

claim: Aversive-driven escape is in equilibrium with freezing behaviors that rely on periaqueductal gray and the amygdala.
source: Aversive-driven escape is in equilibrium with freezing behaviors (innate and learned) that, at least partly, rely on periaqueductal gray and the amygdala (Fadok et al., 2017; Tovote et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Fadok et al., 2017; Tovote et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2015).

claim: Shock-driven LHb excitation and escape behavior are independent of the VTA→LHb projection.
source: We found that shock-driven LHb excitation and escape behavior are independent of the VTA→LHb projection.
evidence: Supported by chemogenetic silencing data showing no effect of VTA→LHb silencing on foot-shock responses (Figure 2C) or escape behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: VTA→LHb terminals activation drives aversive behaviors.
source: However, we report, consistent with published data, that VTA→LHb terminals activation, drives aversive behaviors highlighting that cautious interpretation should be given to motivated behaviors generated by optogenetic manipulation of habenular circuits (Root et al., 2014a; Shabel et al., 2012; Stamatakis et al., 2016; Yoo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic behavioral data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and cited literature (Root et al., 2014a; Shabel et al., 2012; Stamatakis et al., 2016; Yoo et al., 2016).

claim: LH→LHb neurons directly synapse onto 5HT neurons.
source: However, we also find that LH→LHb neurons directly synapse onto 5HT and DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by rabies tracing and electrophysiology data (Figure 3A-B).

claim: LH→LHb neurons directly synapse onto DA neurons.
source: However, we also find that LH→LHb neurons directly synapse onto 5HT and DA neurons.
evidence: Supported by rabies tracing and electrophysiology data (Figure 3A-B).

claim: LH→LHb neurons have relevant control over midbrain GABA neurons.
source: Our data suggest a relevant control by LH→LHb neurons onto midbrain GABA neurons, which in turn may lead to aversion-driven dopamine inhibition (Ungless et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiological data showing strong LH→LHb-to-GABA connectivity and cited literature (Ungless et al., 2004).

claim: LH→LHb control of midbrain GABA neurons may lead to aversion-driven dopamine inhibition.
source: Our data suggest a relevant control by LH→LHb neurons onto midbrain GABA neurons, which in turn may lead to aversion-driven dopamine inhibition (Ungless et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on circuit connectivity and cited literature (Ungless et al., 2004).

claim: The data describe a neural circuit instrumental for escaping a threat.
source: In conclusion, our data describe a neural circuit instrumental for escaping a threat, and open in-depth investigation of cell specificities and synaptic adaptations of the LH→LHb projection to better decipher LHb processing in both health and disease states.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings.

claim: Approximately 50% of LHb neurons recorded are excited by foot-shocks.
source: Foot-shocks (hindpaw delivery) led to fast (~60 ms) and phasic increase (~100 ms) in action potentials in ~50% of neurons recorded across the LHb (Figure 1A–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by pie chart in Figure 1B showing 52% of neurons were foot-shock excited (23/44 neurons).

claim: Foot-shock excited LHb neurons have typical irregular and low bursty firing activity.
source: Note the typical irregular and low bursty firing activity of the LHb Fs encoding neurons (Unpaired t-test, firing rate, t = 4.11, ***p=0.0002; spikes in burst%, t = 2.63, *p=0.011; coefficient of variation%, t = 4.83, ***p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological characterization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D comparing foot-shock excited and not-excited neurons.

claim: LH→LHb connectivity to GABA neurons is approximately 89.2%.
source: Light-evoked glutamatergic/GABAergic currents and connectivity charts for LH→LHb-to-GABA (N/n = 6/28; Connectivity = 89.2%), LH→LHb-to-DA (N/n = 6/29; Connectivity = 79.3%;) and LH→LHb-to-5HT neurons (N/n = 4/27; Connectivity = 55.5%).
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LH→LHb connectivity to DA neurons is approximately 79.3%.
source: Light-evoked glutamatergic/GABAergic currents and connectivity charts for LH→LHb-to-GABA (N/n = 6/28; Connectivity = 89.2%), LH→LHb-to-DA (N/n = 6/29; Connectivity = 79.3%;) and LH→LHb-to-5HT neurons (N/n = 4/27; Connectivity = 55.5%).
evidence: Explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LH→LHb connectivity to 5HT neurons is approximately 55.5%.
